tracks.narration: A single disk gives you one shot at not failing. RAID groups several disks behind one logical drive and trades off speed, capacity, and survival.
RAID zero splits each block across all the disks. Reads and writes go in parallel, so throughput multiplies. But one disk dies and the whole array is lost.
RAID one mirrors every block onto two disks. You lose half your capacity, but a single disk failure leaves a complete copy behind.
RAID five stripes data across all the disks plus one parity stripe — the bitwise xor of the others. Lose any single disk, and the missing stripe can be xor'd back from what's left.
RAID zero buys speed and gambles. RAID one buys safety and pays half. RAID five buys both and pays one disk out of however many you have.
